He ruled that the Festival of Shavuot should always be observed on a Sunday, as it is written in the Torah: _And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the Sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven Sabbaths shall there be complete; even unto the morrow after the seventh Sabbath shall ye number 50 days …_ (Leviticus 23:15–16).[53] He refused to accept the explanation of those who say that one must interpret the words _the morrow after the Sabbath_ here as meaning “the morrow after the holiday,”[54] since we do not find [anywhere] in the Torah that the Sabbath is referred to as a “holiday.”[55] ¶1.324. In the passage: _If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not be married abroad unto one not of his kin; her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of a husband's brother unto her. And it shall be, that the firstborn that she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother that is dead, that his name be not blotted out of Israel_ (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), he interpreted the word _brethren_ as meaning “close relatives” [instead of biological brothers]. For how can we say that the Torah here permits a man [to marry] his brother's wife, when the Torah itself utterly forbids this, when it says:_ Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it is thy brother's nakedness_ (Leviticus 18:16). ¶1.335. R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_ ruled that matzah must be made from barley, because the words _leḥem ʿoni,_ as matzah is called in the Torah (Deuteronomy 16:3), fit two different interpretations: (a) _leḥem ʿoni_—we can interpret it as “bread of affliction,” that is, bread that our ancestors ate in remembrance of the fact that they were afflicted under Egyptian rule for 210 years;[56] (b) _leḥem ʿoni_—we can interpret it as “bread of the poor and destitute,” that is, bread that is generally consumed by the poor and destitute because of its low cost. Such bread is made from barley because they cannot afford to buy bread made from wheat, which is an expensive bread. However, our subsequent sages (of blessed memory) permitted all types of grain for making matzah, namely, [the following] six: (a) wheat, (b) _kussemet_, (c) barley, (d) _shibbolet shuʿal_, (e) _shifon_, and (f) millet[57] (see the book _Adderet_ [_Eliyyahu_], Seder Ḥag ha-Maẓẓot, Chapter 5). Currently, Karaites make their matzah from wheat, and they say that because the eating of matzah is a commandment and because one must accord the commandments great respect, they make it from the more expensive grain—wheat.[58] ¶1.346. He prohibited sexual relations on the Sabbath, on account of what is written in the Torah: _Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest; in plowing time and in harvest thou shalt rest_ (Exodus 34:21). He draws a comparison between plowing and sexual intercourse and permits [the latter] only on weekdays and solely for the purpose of procreation. Therefore, he [also] forbids sexual intercourse with a pregnant woman. And to those who counter with the verse,_ and call the Sabbath a delight_ (Isaiah 58:13), the Karaite sages retort that sexual intercourse [on the Sabbath] leads to weariness and affliction,[59] rather than _delight_.[60] ¶1.357. He opposed with all his might the system of calculations of postponements established by our Rabbanite brethren,[61] who say, for instance, that Passover can never fall on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday;[62] that _ʿAẓeret_ (= Shavuot) can never fall on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday; that Rosh Hashanah can never fall on Sunday, Wednesday, or Friday; that Yom Kippur can never fall on Sunday, Tuesday, or Friday; and that Pur[im] can never fall on Saturday, Monday, or Wednesday. He said that all these are not from the Torah but were fabricated by the sages.}}
content.comments: [48] A lunar month consists of either 29 or 30 days. By convention, a month of 29 days is considered “deficient,” and a month of 30 days is considered “full.” In antiquity, a new month was declared when the crescent new moon was visible to observers. To this day, some observant Karaite Jews still sight the new moon to declare the new month; see the next footnote. | [49] The Festival of Matzah falls in the first month of the biblical calendar, which is the first month after the barley reaches the state of _aviv_. There is no prescribed number of months in the biblical calendar. A year has either 12 or 13 months. By convention, a year with 12 months is considered a regular year, and a year with 13 months is considered a leap year. If, during the twelfth month, the barley is at a stage of ripening called _aviv_ (see Exodus 9:31, Deuteronomy 16:1, et passim), then the year is considered complete, and there is no thirteenth month—the next New Moon signals the first month of the new year. If the barley is not yet _aviv_, then an extra lunar cycle is added, and the new year occurs a month later. Here, Ḥakham Ṭoviyya explains how the Karaites of his day were setting the new year without directly observing the stage of barley ripening. According to the Rabbinic tradition, there are seven leap years interspersed throughout a 19-year cycle. | [50] In contrast to the state of affairs regarding the _aviv_ described by Ḥakham Ṭoviyya, several centuries prior to him, the Karaites in the areas near the Land of Israel would carry out _aviv_ searches each year. See Mordecai b. Nisan_, Royal Attire_, pp. 167–168. | [51] Cf. Jeremiah 24:2. See further below, ¶3.51. | [52] Meton (Athens, fifth century BCE) was a mathematician and astronomer. He is best known for calculations involving the eponymous 19-year Metonic cycle, which he introduced into the so-called lunisolar Attic calendar. The Metonic calendar incorporates knowledge that 19 solar years and 235 lunar months are very nearly equal, such that lunar periods repeat on the same day of the year as 19 years previous. See Robert Hannah, _Greek and Roman Calendars_ (Bristol Classical Press, 2005), pp. 52–71. | [53] Adapted from the JPS translation, with changes to reflect the Karaite understanding of the verse. | [54] The standard Rabbanite interpretation is as follows: the word _Sabbath_ refers to the first day of Passover, and, thus, the counting begins on the second day of Passover, “the morrow after the _Sabbath_,” and Shavuot is observed 49 days after that. See, for example, Babylonian Talmud, _Menaḥot_ 65b. | [55] The phraseology here seems to be reversed; Ḥakham Ṭoviyya means to say that a holiday is never called “the Sabbath” in the Torah, whereas his text says that the Sabbath is never called a “holiday” in the Torah. That said, word order in Hebrew is looser and allows for the subject to come last. In any case, his intent is clear. | [56] Although Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 12:40 state, respectively, that the Israelites spent 400 or 430 years in Egypt, these numbers create a chronological problem when compared to the lifespans of the descendants of Levi in Exodus 6:18–20, 7:7. Kohath was alive when the Israelites entered Egypt (Genesis 46:11), and he lived 133 years. His son Amram lived 137. Amram's son, Moses, was 80 years old in the year of the Exodus. These numbers add up to only 350 years, and presumably there was significant overlap between the lifespans of the fathers and the sons, so the total should be far less. Therefore, the early Rabbanite chronographic work _Seder ʿOlam_ calculates that the 400 years began with the birth of Isaac and that the Israelites spent only 210 of these years actually in Egypt. See _Seder ʿOlam_, ed. Chaim Milikowsky (Jerusalem: Yad Ben-Zvi, 2013), volume 1, p. 226 (ch. 3), and Milikowsky's discussion in volume 2, pp. 55ff. This figure of 210 years is very widely accepted by later Rabbanite writers, and, evidently, was also taken for granted by Ḥakham Ṭoviyya. | [57] Aside from the sixth item (millet), this list of grains that can be used to make matzah is identical to the one in Mishna, _Pesaḥim_ 2:5. Two of the names—_ḥiṭṭa_ (wheat) and _seʿora_ (barley)—are clear, but the identification of the remaining three is controversial. Zohar Amar has written an entire book on the subject (from a Rabbanite-Talmudic, but scientific, point of view): _Five Types of Grain: Historical, Halachic, and Conceptual Aspects_ (Hebrew; Mechon Har Bracha, 2011). | [58] Incidentally, it is worth noting that in the first decades of the twentieth century, the Egyptian government supplied both the Karaite and Rabbanite communities with fine wheat for the production of matzah. This practice was maintained even during World War II, when ordinary commodities were hard to come by. The production of the bread was jointly supervised by representatives of both communities, and each issued its respective seal of approval on the finished product; see Yosef Algamil, _Karaite Jewry in Egypt in Modern Times_ (Ramla: National Council of Karaite Jews in Israel, 1985), English section, p. 15. | [59] This is a pun on the anagrams (words with identical letters, in different orders) _negaʿ_, “affliction,” and _ʿoneg_, “delight” (which already appears in the early medieval work _Sefer Yeẓira_). The word used here for “weariness,” _yegaʿ_, in turn, rhymes with _negaʿ_. | [60] Refraining from sexual intercourse on the Sabbath was not a Karaite innovation. Other non-Rabbinic communities likewise prohibited it, such as the Beta Israel of Ethiopia; see the document “Tĕʾĕzāza Sanbat” in _Falasha Anthology_, ed. and trans. Wolf Leslau (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1951), p. 19. The Beta Israel treat the _Book of Jubilees_ as canonical; this work, from the Second Temple Era, explicitly forbids marital relations on the Sabbath in 50:8: “And the man that does any work on it (the Sabbath) shall die: whoever desecrates that day, whoever lies with (his) wife […] shall die” (R.H. Charles, ed. _The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament in English_, volume II: Pseudepigrapha [Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913], pp. 81f.). In addition, Samaritans, at least in recent centuries, have refrained from sexual intercourse on the Sabbath; see Bernhard Beer, _Das Buch der Jubiläen und sein Verhältniss zu den Midraschim_ (Leipzig: Wolfgang Gerhard, 1856), p. 54, though he notes that Zacharias Frankel believed that this was a later development that Samaritans learned from Karaite Jews. By contrast, the Rabbis of the Talmud recommend the Sabbath as the ideal time for conjugal relations (Babylonian Talmud, _Ketubbot_ 62b). This may have been a reactionary measure against groups that prohibited such activity on the Sabbath. This would not be the only Rabbanite ruling instituted as a reaction to Karaite halakha; as another example, many scholars believe that the Rabbanite custom dating to the Geonic period of reciting a blessing before lighting lamps or candles late on Friday afternoon, to provide light during the Sabbath, began as a reaction to the prevalent Karaite view prohibiting the kindling of such lights. (See, for example, Yitzhak D. Gilat, _Studies in the Development of the Halakha_ [Hebrew; Bar-Ilan University Press, 1992], p. 344.) | [61] The Rabbanites have rules to postpone the celebration of the New Moon by a day if the calculated date will cause certain holidays to fall on certain days of the week. These rules do not appear explicitly in the Talmud, though some vague references to a primitive form of some of them occur in the Babylonian Talmud, _Rosh ha-Shana_ 20a. The formulation cited here is in §428 of the law codes _Ṭur_ and _Shulḥan ʿArukh_. The _Ṭur_ was written in the fourteenth century, and the _Shulḥan ʿArukh_ in the sixteenth, but these rules predate the _Ṭur_ by several hundred years, though they are post-Talmudic. | [62] The days of the week here are all indicated by acronyms. For example, the first acronym is _BaD”U_; that is, Passover may not begin on Monday (the second day of the week, _bet_), Wednesday (the fourth day of the week, _dalet_), or Friday (the sixth day of the week, _vav_). Our author alludes ironically to this acronym when he uses the word “fabricated,” _badu_, later in the sentence, which is also an allusion to I Kings 12:33: _And [Jeroboam] went up unto the altar which he had made in Beth-el on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, even in the month which he had devised [bada] of his own heart […]._

content.hebrew:
והנה מן השריד והפליט מחבורי רבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א הנמצא בידינו, ומן כל מה שכתבו עליו החכמים הבאים אחריו, יהיו מן הנגררים אחריו או מן המתנגדים אליו, ומן תולדות התפתחות דת הקראים נראה בהיר כצהרים, כי ההתחלה היסודית אשר בנה עליה את הקראות, היא התורה הכתובה עצמה, בלי פנות אל תורה שבעל פה, אשר היא כוללת דברי חכמים. וראש דבר רבנו ענן הנשיא היה תמיד: «חַפִּשׂוּ בְּאוֹרַיְתָא שָׁפִּיר, וְאַל תִּשָּׁעֲנוּ עַל דַּעְתִּי». אבל ביחס אל השאלות אשר אין להן תשובות ברורות בתורה, הוא היה מניח להשתמש בהקשים, כמו הקש קל וחמר הקש דמיון או גזרה שוה, ואחרים, בחשבו, כי כל היוצא בהקש מן הכתוב בתורה הוא כאלו כתוב בתורה, והחוקרים אומרים שבזה רבנו ענן הנשיא דָרַך בשביל אבו חניפא הנזכר למעלה, אשר גם הוא היה משתמש בהקשי דמיון או גזרה שוה בפרשו את הקוראן הק׳.
¶1.37אבל במקומות אשר לא היו נמצאות לשאלות תשובות בתורה, וגם לא היו יוצאות בדרכי ההקש הנ״ל, אזי רבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א היה מצַוה להתנהג בדרך «סבל ירשה», ר״ל להתנהג במנהג אשר בו היה מתנהג העם מזמן קדום, רק בתנאי שהמנהג הזה לא יתנגד לרוח התורה.
content.english: Now, from the remnants and relics[63] that we have from R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi's own writings, and from all that later sages—be they followers or opponents—wrote about him, and from the history of the development of the Karaite faith,[64] [one thing] is clear as day: the fundamental basis on which he built Karaism is the Written Torah itself, without resorting to an Oral Law that contains the words of sages. The motto of R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi was always: “Search Scripture well, and do not rely on my opinion” (_ḥappisu be-oraita shappir, ve-ʾal tishaʿanu ʿal daʿti_).[65] However, in regard to matters that do not have clear answers in the Torah, he allowed utilizing the hermeneutical principle of _heqqesh_ (inference); for instance, _heqqesh qal va-ḥomer_ (_argumentum a fortiori_, reasoning from the stronger case to the weaker case); _heqqesh dimyon_ (analogical reasoning); or_ gezera shava_ (reasoning on the basis of similar language), and others. This is because he was of the opinion that all that is derived by _heqqesh_ from the Torah is considered as if it were actually written in the Torah itself. The scholars say that on this point, R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi followed the path of the aforementioned Abu Ḥanifa, who likewise utilized inferences of _dimyon_ and _qal va-ḥomer_ in his explication of the Holy Qurʾan.[66]
content.comments: [63] Cf. Joshua 8:22. | [64] Early Karaite history is still very unclear. As Zvi Cahn has written: “The origin and development of the Karaites are still largely surrounded by mystery and not a little uncertainty…This uncertainty is due to the lack of the historic sense that characterized the Karaites, though they have produced hundreds of books (and even thousands according to their assertions) that have been lost in the course of time” (_The Rise of the Karaite Sect: A New Light on the Halakah and Origin of the Karaites_ [New York: M. Tausner, 1937], p. 37). The various traditions about ʿAnan, who he was, where and when he lived, and whether or not he was the Exilarch or even of the family of the Exilarchate, are all rooted in reports, some of them contradictory, from hundreds of years later. See Moshe Gil, “Karaite Antiquities” (Hebrew), in _Teʿuda_ 15 (1999), pp. 71–107; and idem, “The Origins of the Karaites,” in Meira Polliack (ed.), _Karaite Judaism: A Guide to Its History and Literary Sources_ (Leiden: Brill, 2003), pp. 73–118. | [65] This aphorism's first clause is in Aramaic, and the second clause—influenced by Proverbs 3:5—is in Hebrew. Its origin is shrouded in uncertainty, but its first extant citation is in the commentary of Yefet b. ʿEli to the book of Zechariah. Its origin was possibly in the (now lost) introduction to ʿAnan's _Book of Commandments_. | [66] Ḥakham Ṭoviyya uses the abbreviation _quf_, which apparently stands for _qadosh_, “holy.” One might be surprised to see a Jewish sage use this epithet for the Qurʾan, but it is less surprising given the ecumenical activities of Ḥakham Ṭoviyya. As noted in the introduction, prominent Muslims attended his funeral or expressed condolences.

content.english: However, in those places where one cannot find answers, neither in the Torah nor via the hermeneutical methods, R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_ would command [his followers] to conduct themselves in the way of “the Burden of Inheritance” (_sevel yerusha_); that is, to conduct themselves in accordance with the custom that the people had observed since ancient times, provided that the custom not contravene the spirit of the Torah.[67]
content.comments: [67] In its most narrow sense, the Burden of Inheritance refers to customs and practices that were known at the time the Torah was given and were incorporated by reference in the Torah. For example, we read in Genesis 37:31 that Joseph's brothers slaughtered (from the Hebrew root for _sheḥita_) a goat. From this Karaites derive that (i) the proper way to slaughter was known to ancient Israelites and (ii) the Torah did not need to specify a particular method. This also explains why Karaites do not believe an Oral Torah was necessary to explain how to slaughter.
content.arabic: أما المسائل التي لم يرد عنها جواب في التوراة وليس لها حكم من القياس فكان عنان يوصي باتباع التقاليد «سبيل يروشا» وهو العرف المتبع في قديم الزمان بشرط ألا يناقض روح التوراة.

content.hebrew: ומן כל הנאמר נוכל להוציא כי דת הקראים מיוסדת על שלושה עמודים, והם 1) הכתוב, ר״ל כל מה שכתוב בתורה 2) ההקש 3) וסבל הירושה.
content.english: And from all this, we can conclude that the Karaite faith is based on three main pillars, namely: (i) the written word (that is, all that is written in the Torah); (ii) the [hermeneutical principle of] _heqqesh_; and (iii) the Burden of Inheritance.
content.arabic: من كل ما ذكر نستطيع أن نستنتج أن شريعة القرائين مؤسسة على ثلاث دعائم وهي — أولاً: نص التوراة， ثانياً: القياس， ثالثاً: التقاليد.

content.hebrew:
לנו לדעת כי חרות הדעת בפרוש התורה, אשר הניח ענן הנשיא יר״א לא נתאחרה מלתת פרי טוב, ומיד אחריו קמו בתוך הקראים, ברב מקצועות החכמות הנודעות בימים ההם, חכמים מצוינים, הם היו המיסדים הראשונים את חכמת הדקדוק ואת חכמת הלשון, הם היו בוראי הנקוד ומתקני נקוד הטבראני הם היו מסדרי האגרונות, הם היו בוראי חכמת השואת הלשונות, העברית והערבית והארמית, הם היו המכניסים המשקל והחרוז בשירה, כדרך משוררי ערב, ומהם יצאו משוררים גדולים, מפרשים גדולים, פילוסופים אלהותיים מצוינים, וגם רופאים מומחים וכו׳, וכל זאת לנו לעדות כי דת הקראות איננה מקור הקפאון וההתקרשות, כאשר מוציאים עליה דבה רעה, אלה, אשר עינם רעה בדת הקראים, כי אם להפך היא מקור ההתקדמות וההתפתחות.
וכן כתב החוקר הגדול בספרות הקראים שמחה פינסקער נ״ע בספרו המהלל «לקוטי קדמוניות» (דף ד׳): «נגלו לפנינו מחברים מבעלי מקרא שעמלו בשדה הרחב הזה, וזרעו וקצרו, ועשו פרי בכל מין ממיני ידיעות החיצוניות בתכונה ובפילוסופייה והמליצה והשיר והדקדוק והערכת שרשי לשה״ק בסדר א׳ ב׳ כפי מה שהביאם הצרך להבנת פשטי כה״ק ופירושיהן...»
content.english:
It is important to realize that the principle of freedom of interpretation, as laid down by ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_, soon bore fruit: immediately after him, there arose distinguished scholars among the Karaites, in every single field of scholarship known at the time. They were the first to establish the study of philology and linguistics; they devised the pointing system (_niqqud_) and established the Tiberian [system of] pointing;[68] they compiled lexicons;[69] [and] they invented the study of comparative linguistics, [comparing] Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic. They introduced meter and rhyme into [Hebrew] poetry, in the style of the Arabic poets.[70] They also produced great poets, great exegetes, distinguished theologians,[71] expert physicians, and more.[72] All of this bears testimony to the fact that the Karaite faith is not the source of stagnation and ossification that its detractors, in their antipathy to Karaism, make it out to be, but rather the opposite is true: it is a source of progress and innovation.[73]
And thus wrote the great scholar of Karaite literature, Simḥa Pinsker (may his soul rest in Eden), in his acclaimed _Liqquṭé Qadmoniyyot_ (p. 4): “We have discovered that there were Karaite authors who toiled in this vast field, sowing, reaping, and giving forth fruit in all fields of external knowledge:[74] astronomy, philosophy, rhetoric, poetry, philology, and lexicography,[75] as they needed to do in order to understand the plain words of Scripture and their meanings.”
content.comments: [68] Hebrew, like most other Semitic languages, was originally written as a consonantal skeleton without accompanying signs for the vowels. At some point in the second half of the first millennium CE, various schools of Jewish scholars known as “Masoretes” arose, most famously in Tiberias in the Galilee but also elsewhere. They invented the system of pointing, the diacritical marks indicating vowels, to record the reading traditions of the Bible, which had hitherto been preserved orally. They also worked on preserving other aspects of the biblical text, such as the exact spelling. Though Ḥakham Ṭoviyya writes here that the inventors of the pointing system were Karaites, there is no way to prove this; in fact, both Karaites and Rabbanites were heavily involved in Masoretic activity and shared their work with one another. See Geoffrey Khan, “The Karaites and the Hebrew Bible,” lecture at the Fifteenth International Orion Symposium, “The Texts of the Bible from the Dead Sea Scrolls to the Biblical Manuscripts of the Vienna Papyrus Collection,” April 10, 2016, [[https://www.scribd.com/document/329693162/KHAN-GEOFFREY-15-OrSymp-2016-the-Karaites-and-the-Hebrew-Bible]], retrieved on March 30, 2017. | [69] Ḥakham Ṭoviyya uses the word _egron_ for “lexicon.” This word was invented by the Rabbanite scholar R. Saʿadya Gaʾon, as a calque of the Arabic _jamhara_, “collection”; Saʿadya's word _egron_ is from the Hebrew root _ʾ-g-r_, “to collect.” See Neḥemya Allony (ed.), _Ha-Egron: Kitāb ʾUṣūl al-Shiʿr al-ʿIbrānī_ (Hebrew; Jerusalem: Academy of the Hebrew Language, 1969), pp. 17f. and 87f.; on 17f., Allony lists six later works that used Saʿadya's term _egron_ as part of their title, at least one of which is by a Karaite author, ʿAli b. Suleiman. | [70] In fact, Karaite poets were not the originators of either rhyme or syllabic meter in Hebrew poetry, as Ḥakham Ṭoviyya implies here with the word _makhnisim_, “introduced.” Rhyme was used in Hebrew poetry starting with the great Rabbanite poets of the sixth century CE, such as Yannai, long before the time of ʿAnan, and it has been present in most Hebrew poetry since. (See Ezra Fleischer, “_Beḥinnot be-Tahalikh ʿAliyyat he-Ḥaruz ba-Shira ha-ʿIvrit ha-Qeduma_,” _Meḥqeré Yerushalayim be-Sifrut ʿIvrit_ 1 [1981], pp. 226–238.) On the other hand, syllabic meters, in the style of the Arabic poets, were introduced into Hebrew poetry in the tenth century by Dunash b. Labraṭ, who was a student of the great Rabbanite scholar and poet Saʿadya Gaʾon. (See Jefim Schirmann and Ezra Fleischer, _The History of Hebrew Poetry in Muslim Spain_ [Hebrew; Jerusalem: Magnes Press and Ben-Zvi Institute, 1995], pp. 119–122.) Babovich is not the first to make the claim that Karaite poets preceded Dunash in using such meters in Hebrew; Simḥa Pinsker stated this in his _Liqquṭé Qadmoniyyot_ (Vienna: Adalbert della Torre, 1860), p. 4, without any real evidence. This is probably related to Pinsker's misdating of R. Moses Darʿi to the mid-ninth century rather than the mid-twelfth; see Joachim Yeshaya, _Medieval Hebrew Poetry in Muslim Egypt:__ The Secular Poetry of the Karaite Poet Moses b. Abraham Darʿī_ (Leiden: Brill, 2011), pp. 11f. Babovich was familiar with Pinsker's work, and in this very paragraph, he quotes a passage from the same page, so he presumably also obtained this idea from him (and, as we will see below, in ¶1.45, he follow Pinsker's dating of R. Moses Darʿi to the ninth century). In any event, later Karaite poets certainly used syllabic meters and rhyme in their Hebrew poetry. | [71] The term for divinity (_elohut_, or _elohi_) is often used in Hebrew writing of the past millennium in reference to the work of theologians, even non-Jewish ones, and later on, to kabbalists as well. See Yaakov Shmuel Spiegel, _ʿAmmudim be-Toledot ha-Sefer ha-ʿIvri_, vol. 3 (Jerusalem, 2014), pp. 149–154. | [72] Note that the Hebrew text continues with the following sentences, but the Arabic text of the original publication of _Rosh Pinna_ ends this paragraph here. The omitted text appears in the original Arabic publication of _Rosh Pinna_ in what we have designated as paragraph 1.51. In order to harmonize the Arabic and Hebrew, we have moved the Arabic text to paragraph 1.39 in our edition. | [73] This is not the only place where Ḥakham Ṭoviyya writes adamantly about this point. He writes similarly in the introduction to his halakhic work, _Ḥuqqé ha-Peraṭ la-ʿAdat ha-Qaraʾim be-Miẓrayim_: “Our lips will grow weary if we continue to demonstrate that the favorite dictum of the founder of our community, R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_, `Search Scripture well, and do not rely on my opinion,' shows with certainty that Karaism is based on free thinking and is not a source of archaism and unyielding rigidity, as is claimed by those who are hostile to Karaism. On the contrary, it is a source of development, and it leaves great space for progress, in accordance with the place and time.” Babovich did not succeed in publishing this work in his lifetime; after his death, it was found among his papers by Yosef Algamil, who published it in his collection of Babovich's writings, _Pirqé Ṭoviyya_, vol. 2, pp. 253–349. Our quote appears on p. 264. For the story of Algamil's discovery of the work, see p. 273, footnote 1. | [74] The term “external knowledge” probably means here, as it often does in Hebrew literature, secular branches of scholarship. | [75] Literally, “arranging Hebrew roots alphabetically.”
content.arabic: ويجب علينا أن نعرف أن حرية الرأي أو الاجتهاد في تفسير التوراة وقد أخذ بها عنان قد أتت ثمارها سريعاً بعد وفاته. إذ قام في وسط القرائين في كثير من الدوائر العلمية المعروفة في تلك الأيام علماء بارزون كانوا أوائل المؤسسين لعلوم اللغة والنحو والصرف في العبرية وهم الذين ابتدعوا الحركات أي (الشكل) ونظموا الحركات الطبريانية ووضعوا القواميس وأول من كشف القرابة بين اللغات العبرية والعربية والآرامية， وهم الذين اقتبسوا عن العرب الوزن والقافية في الشعر العبري ولقد كان منهم فحول الشعراء وأعاظم الفقهاء والمفسرين. والفلاسفة في علم اللاهوت كما كان أيضاً منهم مهرة الأطباء ذوو الشهرة الذائعة وغير ذلك من العلوم. كل هذا يشهد بأن شريعة القرائين ليست منبعاً للجمود والتحجر كما يفتري عليها الكارهون لها بل بالعكس هي منبع للتطور وللتقدم وبهذا شهد (سمحا بنسكر) البحاثة العظيم في آداب القرائين في كتابه المشهور (لقوطي قدمونيوت) ومعناه «مجمع الآثار» فقد ورد في صفحة ١٤ من هذا الكتاب ما يأتي: اتضح لنا مؤلفون من القرائين جاهدوا في هذا الحقل الواسع وزرعوا وحصدوا وأنتجوا ثمرة في كل نوع من أنواع العلوم الدنيوية كالفلك والفلسفة والبلاغة والشعر والنحو وترتيب القواميس العبرية بحسب الحروف الأبجدية حيث اضطرهم لذلك وجوب فهم الكتاب المقدس وتفسيره.

content.hebrew:
ולמען לא יהיו דברי אלה, כדברים התלואים באויר, אחשוב לנכון להזכיר פה קצת מן שמות חכמי הקראים היותר מצוינים במקצוע החכמות הנזכרות למעלה, והם שמות רק הקדמונים מהם עד המאה XV, ואם יהיה לי פנאי ובעת רצון, אם יעזרני השם, אשתדל לעשות חבור על ספרות הקראים בכלל, אשר בו אביא שמות כל חכמי הקראים, הקדמונים והחדשים, המפורסמים והבלתי מפורסמים. אבל כעת אסתפק בהביא רק שמות חכמי הקראים המצוינים מהקדמונים, ואלה הם:
{{quote:I. ¶1.41בחכמת הדקדוק. יהודה בן קוריש מן פאס (מאה IX), אבו אלפרג אהרן הנודע בשם המדקדק איש ירושלם (מאה IX), יהודה בן עלן מן טברייא (מאה X), (והוא הוא, אשר כפי דעת החכם ר׳ שמחה פינסקער, הסופר הערבי מסעודי, עלי אבול חסאן, שנפטר 926 למה״נ, קוראו בל׳ ערבית יחיי בן (= אבו) זכריה הכותב). II. ¶1.42במליצה. רבנו סלמון בן ירוחים (מאה X), רבנו נסי בן נח (מאה X), רבנו סהל בן מצליח הכהן, הנקרא אבו סרי (מאה X), רבנו חסון בן מצליח הקרא (מאה X), רבנו טוביה העובד (מאה XI), רבנו משה הכהני (מאה XI). III. ¶1.43בוראי ומתקני הנקוד הטבראני. בן אשר (מאה X), רב מוחה (מאה X), ובנו משה בן מוחה (מאה XI), יהודה בן משה הנקדן המזרחי בן יהודה הגבור (מאה X?). IV. ¶1.44מסדרי האגרונות. דוד בן אברהם אלפאסי (מאה X), מנחם בן סרוק (מאה XI), עלי בן סוליימן (מאה XI). V. ¶1.45משוררים גדולים. ר׳ משה דרעי (מאה IX), מבורך בן נתן בן ניסן הלוי (מאה IX), אדונים בן ר׳ מסימן הלוי ובנו ר׳ משה (מאה IX), ר׳ יהודה בן עלאן הטבראני (מאה X), ישראל הדַיָּן הראשון האסכנדרי בן ר׳ דניאל המערבי (מאה XI), ר׳ כלב אפנדופולי (מאה XV). VI. ¶1.46מפרשים גדולים על התנ״ך. רבנו דניאל בן משה קומיסי או דמאגאני (מאה IX), רבנו יפת המלמד הגדול (מאה X), רבנו יוסף בן נח (מאה XI), רבנו יעקב בן ראובן (מאה XI), רבנו אהרן הראשון הרופא בן יוסף (מאה XIII), רבנו אהרן האחרון בן אליהו ניקומידיאו (מאה XIV). VII. ¶1.47מפרשים גדולים על המצות. רבנו דניאל בן משה קומיסי או דמאגאני (מאה IX), רבנו לוי הלוי הנקרא אבו האשם בן רבנו יפת המלמד הגדול (מאה X), רבנו ישועה בן יהודה הנקרא אבו אלפרג פורקן אבו אסד (מאה XI), ותלמידו אבן תראס מן קסטילייא באיספנייה (מאה XI) (עליו מספרים שאשתו ג״כ היתה אשה מלומדת, ואחרי מות אישה, אנשי הקהלה היו פונים אליה בשאלות בעניני הדת, והיו שומעים בקולה כשמוע בקול נביא השם, והיתה מפורסמת אצלם בשם «מלמדת» «מועללימה» בל׳ ערבית). רבנו יהודה הדסי (מאה XII) ר׳ ישראל הדין השני בן שמואל המערבי ותלמידו ר׳ יפת הרופא בן דוד בן שמואל בן צעיר (מאה XIII), ר׳ שמואל המערבי (מאה XIV), ר׳ אליהו בשייצי (מאה XV). VIII. ¶1.48בחכמת הרפואה. ר׳ משה דרעי (מאה IX), אבו באיאן אל מודבבר ושמו בעברית שלמה בן ישראל, והוא היה רופא של המלך שולטן סלח דין האיובי (מאה XII) ובנו אבו פדל דאווד ושמו בעברית דוד בן שלמה (מאה XII) (לדוד בן שלמה חבורים רבים בחכמת הרפואה, ומהם מפורסם חבורו «חקי סמי הרפואה המרכבים», ובערבית «دستور الادوية المركبة». החבור הזה בכתב יד נמצא בבית עקד הספרים בעיר אוקספורד באנגלייא, בעיר מינכין באלמנייא, ובעיר אלקאהרה פה. הוא היה רופא של המלך שולטן אלמליכ אל אביל אבו בכר בן אל איוב. והרופא המפורסם הערבי אבן אבי אוסייבייא, אשר חבר ספר גדול בשם «תולדות הרופאים» היה תלמידו ועמיתו) ר׳ אהרן הראשון הרופא בן יוסף (מאה XIII), ור׳ יפת הרופא בן דוד בן שמואל בן צעיר הנקרא «אלחכים אלצפי» (מאה XIII) ור׳ אליהו בשייצי (מאה XV). IX. ¶1.49פילוסופים אלהותיים. ר׳ בנימן נהאונדי (מאה IX), רבנו מנחם ניצני הגולה בן מיכאל (מאה IX), דוד בן מרוואן הבבלי הערקי, הנודע אלמקמץ (מאה IX), רבנו יוסף הרואה בן אברהם הנקרא יוסף אלבציר (והוא ישראל ולא כהן, כאשר כתבו קצת החכמים בטעות) (מאה XI), ר׳ אהרן האחרון ניקומידיאו (מאה XIV). X. ¶1.50בתולדות הכתות הדתיות בישראל. יעקב בן יצחק בן שמעיה אלקרקסאני, הנקרא אבו יוסוף יעקב (מאה X), והוא יחיד במינו בכתיבת תולדות, יען לא היה ממנהג חכמינו הקדמונים לכתוב תולדות, ורבנו זה יעקב אלקרקסאני (קרקסאן מקום אצל בגדד) היה חכם גדול גם בחכמה הדתית, והיה ג״כ מפרש גדול וכל חבוריו כתב בל׳ ערבית. המציון [צ״ל המצוין] בהם חבורו «כתאב אלאַנואר ואלמרקיב» (ס׳ המאורות והמגדלים) בשלושה עשר מאמרים. XI. ¶1.51שמות כל חכמי הקראים. אבן אלהיתי (המאה XV) חבר ספר בל׳ ערבית, הביא בו שמות כל חכמי הקראים, והאחרון שבהם רבנו שמואל הרופא בן משה המערבי, בע״ס המצות הנודע בשם אלמרשיד, ובל׳ הק׳ «המישר». אשר חברו בש׳ 5194 לבריאה, והוא 1434 למה״נ. ס׳ אבן אלהיתי נדפס ע״י החכם מרגליות בלונדון הבירה בש׳ 1897 למה״נ.}}
content.english:
So that what I have said not remain abstract, I think that it would be proper here to name some of the more distinguished Karaite scholars who excelled in the various fields mentioned above. [I will limit this list] exclusively to the names of the earlier ones, [who flourished up until] the fifteenth century; if I have the leisure, and it is an opportune time, with God's help, I will make an effort to write another work on Karaite literature in general, in which I will enumerate the names of all the Karaite sages, from antiquity to the present, the well known and the obscure. But right now I will content myself with mentioning only the names of a few distinguished early Karaite sages, namely, the following:
{{quote:I. ¶1.41^^Philologists:^^ Judah b. Quraysh from Fez (ninth century);[76] Abu al-Faraj Aaron, who is known as “the grammarian from Jerusalem” (tenth century); Judah b. ʿAlan of Tiberias (tenth century) (according to R. Simḥa Pinsker, he is to be identified with Yaḥya b. [rather, Abu] Zakariya the Writer, who is mentioned in Arabic by the Arab writer Masʿudi ʿAli Abu ʾl-Ḥasan, who died in 926). II. ¶1.42^^Rhetoricians:^^ R. Salmon b. Yeruḥim (tenth century);[77] R. Nissi b. Noah (tenth century); R. Sahl b. Maẓliaḥ ha-Kohen, who is called “Abu Sari” (tenth century); R. Ḥasun b. Maẓliaḥ the Caller[78] (tenth century); R. Tobias ha-ʿOved (eleventh century); and R. Moses ha-Kohani (eleventh century). III. ¶1.43^^Inventors of the Tiberian Vocalization System:^^ Ben Asher (tenth century);[79] Rav Muḥa (tenth century) and his son Moses b. Muḥa (eleventh century); and Judah b. Moses the Vocalizer of the East b. Judah ha-Gibbor (tenth century?). IV. ¶1.44^^Lexicographers:^^ David b. Abraham al-Fasi (tenth century); Menaḥem b. Saruq[80] (eleventh century); ʿAli b. Suleiman (eleventh century). V. ¶1.45^^Major Poets:^^ R. Moses Darʿi (ninth century);[81] Mevorakh b. Nathan b. Nisan ha-Levi (ninth century); Adonim b. R. Mesiman ha-Levi and his son R. Moses (ninth century); R. Judah b. ʿAlan of Tiberias (tenth century); Israel ha-Dayyan[82] I of Alexandria b. R. Daniel ha-Maʿaravi (eleventh century); R. Caleb Afendopolo (fifteenth century). VI. ¶1.46^^Major Expositors of the Bible:^^ R. Daniel b. Moses al-Qumisi or Damaghani (ninth century); R. Yefet the Great Teacher (tenth century); R. Joseph b. Noah (eleventh century); R. Jacob b. Reuben (eleventh century); R. Aaron I the Physician b. Joseph (thirteenth century); R. Aaron the Younger b. Elijah of Nicomedia (fourteenth century). VII. ¶1.47^^Major Expositors of the Commandments^^: R. Daniel b. Moses al-Qumisi or Damaghani (ninth century); R. Levi ha-Levi, who is called “Abu Hashim” b. R. Yefet the Great Teacher (tenth century); R. Yeshuʿa b. Judah, who is known as “Abu al-Faraj Furqan Abu Asad” (eleventh century) and his disciple Ibn Taras, from Castile in Spain (eleventh century).[83] (Regarding the latter, it is related that his wife was a learned woman, and after his death, the members of the community would turn to her with any queries about religion, and they would listen to her as one listens to a prophet of God. She was famously known among them as “the [female] teacher”—_al-Muʿallima_ in Arabic.)[84] R. Judah Hadassi (twelfth century); R. Israel ha-Dayyan II b. Samuel ha-Maʿaravi[85] and his disciple R. Yefet the Physician b. David b. Samuel b. Ẓaʿir (thirteenth century); R. Samuel ha-Maʿaravi (fourteenth century); and R. Elijah Bašyachi (fifteenth century). VIII. ¶1.48^^Medical Scholars:^^ R. Moses Darʿi (ninth century); Abu Bayan al-Mudabbir, whose Hebrew name was Solomon b. Israel, and who was personal physician to Sultan Saladin the Ayyubid (twelfth century) and his son Abu Fadl Daʾud, whose Hebrew name was David b. Solomon (twelfth century). (The latter composed several treatises on medicine, one of the most famous of which is _The Rules of Medicinal Compounds_ (in Arabic: _Dustūr al-Adwiyya al-Murakkaba_). This manuscript is currently held by the library in Oxford, England, and [also] in the city of Munich, Germany,[86] as well as here in Cairo. He was personal physician to the Sultan al-Malik al-Abil Abu Bakr bin al-Ayyub.[87] The renowned Arab physician Ibn Abu Usibiyya, who composed the long _History of Physicians_, was his pupil and colleague.)[88] R. Aaron I the Physician b. Joseph (thirteenth century); R. Yefet the Physician b. David b. Samuel b. Ẓaʿir, who is called “al-Ḥakim al-Ṣafī” (thirteenth century); and R. Elijah Bašyachi (fifteenth century). IX. ¶1.49^^Theologians:^^ R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi (ninth century); R. Menaḥem Niẓani ha-Golé b. Michael (ninth century); David b. Marwan of Babylon-Iraq, who is known as “al-Muqammiṣ” (ninth century);[89] R. Joseph the Seer b. Abraham, known as “Joseph al-Baṣir”[90] (he was an Israelite[91] and not, as some scholars have mistakenly written, a priest) (eleventh century); R. Aaron the Latter of Nicomedia (fourteenth century). X. ¶1.50^^Historiographers of Jewish Religious Sects:^^ Jacob b. Isaac b. Shemaya al-Qirqisani, who is called “Abu Yusuf Yaʿqub” (tenth century), was unique in that he wrote histories, for it was not generally customary among our early sages to engage in this particular endeavor. This teacher of ours, Jacob al-Qirqisani ([from] Qirqisān, a place near Baghdad), was also a great religious scholar and a great exegete. He composed all his works in Arabic; the most notable of them is his work _Kitāb_ _al-Anwār wa-al-Marāqib_ (_The Book of Lights and Watchtowers_) in 13 parts.[92] XI. ¶1.51^^Enumerators of the Karaite Sages:^^ Ibn al-Hiti (fifteenth century) authored a work in Arabic in which he lists the names of all the Karaite sages. The last is R. Samuel the Physician b. Moses ha-Maʿaravi, the author of the _Book of Commandments_, which is called _al-Murshīd_ and in Hebrew_ Ha-Meyasher_ (“the one that makes straight”), which he wrote in the year 5194 from Creation, which corresponds to 1434 CE. Ibn al-Hiti's book was published by the scholar Margoliouth in London in 1897.[93]}}
content.comments: [76] I have retained Ḥakham Ṭoviyya's designation of which centuries these scholars lived; however, it would behoove the reader to independently verify some of these dates, as subsequent scholarship has clarified the correct time frames. | [77] Here, Ḥakham Ṭoviyya makes reference to the Karaite sage known as “Salmon b. Yeruḥam” or “Salomon b. Yeruḥim.” Salmon's most notable achievement is his polemic against R. Saʿadya Gaʾon, entitled _Sefer Milḥamot Adonai_ (_The Book of the Wars of the Lord_), which has been edited and published by Israel Davidson (New York: Jewish Theological Seminary of America, 1934). | [78] The Hebrew ha-Qoré (or possibly ha-Qara) apparently indicates that this sage actively called upon his fellow Jews to take action, possibly by returning to the land of Israel or by returning to the Torah. | [79] There was a large Ben Asher family of Masoretes, of whom the most famous was Aaron Ben Asher. Much ink has been spilled over the question of whether they were Karaites or Rabbanites. See Khan, “The Karaites and the Hebrew Bible” (above in ¶1.39, footnote 61), who cites some of the scholarly literature on the topic. Evidently, Ḥakham Ṭoviyya believed that they were Karaites. Raphael Zer takes the position that the Masorete of the Aleppo Codex was indeed a Karaite, but his article on the topic remains agnostic on whether the Masorete was Aaron Ben Asher. See Raphael Zer, “Was the Masorete of the Aleppo Codex Rabbinical or Karaite?” (Hebrew), _Sefunot_ N.S. 8 (23), (2003), pp. 573–587 and “Was the Masorete of the Aleppo Codex of Rabbanite or of Karaite Origin?” _Textus_ 24 (2009) pp. 239–262. | [80] Standard scholarship has always numbered Menaḥem b. Saruq among the Rabbanites, so it is surprising to see Babovich list him here. The evolution of this claim is as follows. The famous Rabbanite scholar Samuel David Luzzatto (known as “Shadal,” 1800–1865) theorizes, in his article “Menaḥem b. Saruq and Ḥasdai b. Isaac” (Hebrew) (in Luzzatto, _Bet ha-Oẓar_ [Lemberg: Eva Grossmann, 1847], folio 33b) that Menaḥem's antagonist Ḥasdai persecuted him because Ḥasdai suspected him of being a Karaite. Luzzatto writes that suspicions of Saruq's Karaism were floating around in the nineteenth century, and he deduces from a close reading of Menaḥem's epistle to Ḥasdai that this was Ḥasdai's accusation against Menaḥem. However, Luzzatto writes that these suspicions were utterly unfounded (ibid., folio 34b). Nonetheless, Pinsker (_Liqquṭé Qadmoniyyot_, p. 168) adopts Luzzatto's theory but says that the suspicions were correct that Menaḥem did, indeed, hold some Karaite views in his heart, though he was socially part of the Rabbanite community and prayed in the Rabbanite synagogues. As we have seen above (¶1.23, ¶1.39), Babovich owed a great debt to Pinsker's work and considered it historically reliable, so this must be the source of his odd inclusion of Menaḥem in this list of important Karaites. | [81] The works of Moses Darʿi have recently been published in critical editions by Joachim Yeshaya: _Medieval Hebrew Poetry_ and _Poetry and Memory in Karaite Prayer:__ The Liturgical Poetry of the Karaite Poet Moses b. Abraham Darʿī_ (Leiden: Brill, 2014). In 1934, none other than Ḥakham Ṭoviyya Babovich named a synagogue in Cairo, which had been built in the 1920s, after Moses Darʿi; this attests to the ongoing importance of this medieval figure to the leaders of the modern Karaite community (Yeshaya, _Medieval Poetry_, p. 51). Modern scholarship dates Moses Darʿi to the mid-twelfth century, not the mid-ninth; see above in ¶1.39, footnote 63. | [82] A judge in a religious court. | [83] According to the twelfth-century Rabbanite historian Abraham ibn Daud, this Ibn Taras did not start out as a Karaite but was won over to Karaism by Yeshuʿa. (See Ibn Daud, _The Book of Tradition_, pp. 94ff.) | [84] The sentence regarding _al-Muʿallima_ appears in a footnote in the original Arabic publication of _Rosh Pinna_. In order to harmonize the Arabic and Hebrew, we have moved the footnote into the main Arabic text of paragraph 1.47 in our edition. | [85] The Karaite Press has published a translation of R. Israel ha-Dayyan's treatises on slaughter and the principles of faith, together with a critical edition of the Judeo-Arabic. (See _The Karaite Creed and Discourse on Slaughter_, ed. Raphael Dascalu, trans. Raphael Dascalu and James Walker [Daly City: The Karaite Press], 2018.) | [86] The author uses the French name for Germany, “Allemagne.” | [87] Known more simply as “Al-Adil I” or “Sayf al-Din” (1145–1218), he was the younger brother and successor to Saladin. | [88] The words beginning with “The latter” through “pupil and colleague” appear in a footnote in the original Arabic publication of _Rosh Pinna_. In order to harmonize the Arabic and Hebrew, we have moved the footnote into the main Arabic text of paragraph 1.48 in our edition. | [89] Although many Karaites have considered al-Muqqamiṣ to be Karaite, we have no evidence that al-Muqqamiṣ was affiliated with either the Karaites or the Rabbanites. Indeed, al-Qirqisani, the famed tenth-century Karaite, in his _Kitāb al-Anwār wa-al-Marāqib_, simply refers to al-Muqqamiṣ as a Jew. | [90] He was known euphemistically as “the Seer” (ha-Roʾé) because he was blind; his substantial writings (including several polemics, one against the Samaritan sanctification of Mount Gerizim and another against Islam, as well as responsa) were written via dictation. Al-Baṣir was born in Basra, Iraq and later moved to Jerusalem, where he studied at the academy of Joseph ibn Nuḥ. (See Marina Rustow, _Scripture and Schism_, p. 75.) | [91] That is, an ordinary Jew, of neither priestly nor Levitical descent. | [92] One of the foremost scholars of Karaitica, Leon Nemoy (1901–1997) published this monumental work in Arabic (New York: Alexander Kohut Memorial Foundation, 1939–1943). A properly translated and annotated edition remains a scholarly desideratum. | [93] He refers to the orientalist George Margoliouth (1853–1924), who edited and published the work as “Ibn al-Hītī's Arabic Chronicle of Karaite Doctors,” _Jewish Quarterly Review_ IX (1897): pp. 429ff.

وتأييداً لكلامي أذكر فيما يلي بعضاً من أسماء علماء القرائين البارزين في العلوم المذكورة آنفاً وهم قدماء العلماء الذين عاشوا إلى نهاية القرن الخامس عشر. وإذا اتسع لي الوقت في المستقبل سأحاول أن أضع إن شاء الله كتاباً في آداب القرائين العام أسرد فيه جميع أسماء علماء القرائين القدماء والمحدثين المشهورين وغير المشهورين أما الآن فاقتصر على ذكر علماء القرائين القدماء البارزين وهم.
{{quote:.I ¶1.41**في علم الصرف والنحو:** يهوذا ابن قريش من مدينة فاس (القرن التاسع) أبو الفرج هارون الشهير بالنحوي من أورشليم (القرن التاسع) يهوذا ابن علن من طبرية (القرن العاشر) يقول سمحا بنسكر: «وهو من كبار علماء إخواننا الربانين أن العالم العربي المسعودي علي أبو الحسن المتوفي سنة ٩٥٦ م ذكر اسم يحيى للكاتب الطبرياني ابن زكريا وفي رأي سمحا بنسكر أنه هو يهوذا ابن علن نفسه. .II ¶1.42**أعلام البيان والبلاغة:** سلمون بن يروحيم (القرن العاشر) نسي بن نوح (القرن العاشر) سهل بن مصليح الكوهين الشهير بأبي سري (القرن العاشر) حسون بن مصليح القرا (القرن العاشر) طوبيا العابد (القرن الحادي عشر) مرسي الكوهني (للقرن الحادي عشر). .III ¶1.43**واضعو ومرتبو الحركة الطبريانية:** ابن اشير (القرن العاشر) راب موحاه (القرن العاشر) وابنه موسى بن موحاه (القرن الحادي عشر) يهوذا بن موسى النقدان المزراحي بن يهوذا الجبار (القرن العاشر؟). .IV ¶1.44**واضعو القواميس:** داود بن أبراهام الفاسي (القرن العاشر) مناحم بن ساروق (القرن الحادي عشر) علي بن سليمان (القرن الحادي عشر). .V ¶1.45**فحول الشعراء:** ربي موسى الدرعي (القرن التاسع) مبوراح بن ناتان بن نيسان هليفي (القرن التاسع) أدونيم بن مسيماز ليفي， وابنه ربي موشى (القرن التاسع) يهوذا بن علن الطبري (القرن العاشر) إسرائيل هديان الأول الإسكندري بن ربي دانيئيل المغربي (القرن الحادي عشر) ربي كاليف افندبولى (القرن الخامس عشر). .VI ¶1.46**أكابر المفسرين للكتاب المقدس:** دانيئيل بن موسى القميصي أو الدمجاني (القرن التاسع) أستاذنا يافت المعلم الكبير (القرن العاشر) يوسف بن نوح (القرن الحادي عشر) يعقوب بن روبين (القرن الحادي عشر) هارون الأول الطبيب بن يوسف (القرن الثالث عشر) هارون الثاني بن إلياهو نيكوميديو (القرن الرابع عشر). .VII ¶1.47**مشاهير الفقهاء:** دانيئيل بن موسى القميصي أو الدمجاني (القرن التاسع) أستاذنا ليفي هليفي بن يافت المعلم الكبير المكنى بأبي هاشم (القرن العاشر) يشوعا بن يهوذا الشهير بأبي الفرج فرقان بن الأسد (القرن الحادي عشر) وتلميذه بن ترس من كاستيليا «إسبانيا» (القرن الحادي عشر). (يروى عنه أن زوجته كانت أيضاً على جانب عظيم من الثقافة الدينية وبعد وفاة زوجها كانت الطائفة ترجع إليها في المسائل الدينية وكانوا يأخذون برأيها كما لو كان صادراً عن زوجها وكانت مشهورة عندهم باسم «المعلمة».) يهوذا هداسي (القرن الثاني عشر) الأستاذ إسرائيل الديان الثاني بن شمويل المغربي وتلميذه يافت الطبيب بن دافيد بن شمويل بن صغير (القرن الثالث عشر) شمويل المغربي (القرن الرابع عشر) إلياهو بشياصي (القرن الخامس عشر). .VIII ¶1.48**في علوم الطب:** موسى الدرعي «القرن التاسع» أبو البيان المدور واسمه في العبرية شلومو بن إسرائيل وكان طبيباً خاصاً للسلطان صلاح الدين الأيوبي (القرن الثاني عشر) وابنه أبو الفضل داود واسمه في العبرية دافيد بن شلومو (القرن الثاني عشر). (لهذا العالم «دافيد بن شلمو» مؤلفات كثيرة في علم الطب منها كتابه الشهير «دستور الأدوية المركبة» وهذا الكتاب بخط اليد وتوجد منه نسخة في كل من مكتبة جامعة أكسفورد بإنجلترا وفى ميونيخ بألمانيا والقاهرة بدار الكتب الملكية. وكان طبيباً خاصاً للسلطان المليك الأبيل أبي بكر بن أيوب， وقد كان الطبيب العربي المشهور ابن أبي أوسيبيا مؤلف كتاب «تاريخ الأطباء» تلميذاً وصديقاً له.) الأستاذ هارون الأول الطبيب بن يوسف (القرن ١٣) الأستاذ يافت بن دافيد بن شموئيل ابن صغير الشهير بالحكيم الصافي (القرن ١٣) الأستاذ إلياهو بشياصي (القرن ١٥). .IX ¶1.49**الفلاسفة وعلماء اللاهوت:** بنيامين النهاوندي (القرن ٩) مناحم‏ بن جيتشني المهاجر بن ميخائيل (القرن ٩) دافيد بن مروان البابلي العراقي الشهير باسم المقمص (القرن ٩) يوسف هرؤى بن أبراهام الشهير بيوسف البصير وهو من إسرائيل وليس كوهين كما ذكر بعض العلماء خطأ (القرن ١١) هارون الثاني نيكوميديو (القرن ١٤). .X ¶1.50**في تاريخ المذاهب:** يعقوب بن إسحق بن شمعيا القرقساني «من العراق» الشهير بأبي يوسف يعقوب (القرن ١٠) وهو وحيد في نوعه في كتب التاريخ إذ لم يكن من عادة علمائنا القدماء تدوين الحوادث التاريخية أما أستاذنا هذا يعقوب القرقساني فكان عالماً عظيماً في اللاهوت كما كان من أكابر المفسرين وقد كتب كل مصنفاته باللغة العربية أشهرها كتاب «الأنوار والمراقب» ويحتوى على ١٣ مقالة. .XI ¶1.51**في تسجيل أسماء علماء القرائين:** ابن الهيتي من القرن الخامس عشر وضع كتاباً سجل فيه أسماء جميع علماء القرائين وآخرهم أستاذنا شموئيل الطبيب بن موسى المغربي مؤلف كتاب الوصايا باللغة العربية «المرشد» وترجم إلى العبرية باسم «هَمّْيَاشِير» وقد ألفه سنة ٥١٩٤ للخليقة — ١٤٣٤ إفرنجية وقد تولى طبع سجل ابن الهيتي العالم الإنكليزي مرجليوت سنة ١٨٩٧ بمدينة لندن.}}

content.hebrew:
ונביא פה לזכרון את דברי הסופר המצוין בין סופרי תולדות בתוך חכמי הערבים, הוא תאקי אלדין אחמד אבן עלי מקריזי (המאה XIV) אשר כתב על רבנו ענן הנשיא, ואלה הם (בתרגום ר׳ שמחה פינסקער)
{{quote:אמנם הענניים הנה הם מיוחסים אל ענן ראש גליות, שבא מן המזרח בימי אבו געפר אלמנצור, ועמו נסח המשנה תורה, שנעתקה מכתיבת יד של הנביא משה ע״ה, וכשראה מה שהיה עליו מן היהודים הרבנים והקראים מתנגדים למה שבידו, עצר כח יחידי להתקומם נגדם וטען עליהם בדתיהם, והיה נכבד אצלם וחשבוהו מיוצאי חלציו של דהע״ה ולאיש היותר חסיד בבחינת הדת, וחשבו שאלו היה בזמן הבית היה נביא, ולא יכלו להרים ראש נגדו, לפי שהיה חוץ ממה שזכרנו, חשוב בעיני הכליף שכבדהו מאד, וממה שהתחלף בו מן היהודים הוא עשית החדשים עפ״י הראיה, כמו שהוא ג״כ בדת האיסלם ולא חש באיזה יום מן השבוע חל החדש, ועזב חשבון הרבנים ועִבור החדשים ואמר שטעו בזה וסמך בו רק על מציאת האביב בשעורים (ראה חלק שני מספרו «אלכטאט» (השבילים) השער «כתות היהודים כעת»).}}

צריך להעיר פה, כי מה שאמר מקריזי, מן היהודים הרבנים והקראים מתנגדים למה שבידו, אמת הדבר, כי נמצאים מן החכמים הקדמונים מן הקראים שהתנגדו בקצת לענן הנשיא, ר״ל לא הסכימו לדעתו בכל מקום, אבל כל זה ביחס אל הענפים ולא אל השרשים, כי בדברים יסודיים של הדת, כלם היו מסכימים עמו.
content.english: It is important to note here that what al-Maqrizi said about both Rabbanites and Karaites being opposed to “what was in his hands” is true. Some early Karaites opposed ʿAnan on some matters; in other words, they did not agree with him on everything, but all [these disagreements] related only to the branches and not to the roots, for they were all in agreement with him regarding the main tenets of the movement.[94]
content.comments: [94] The Hebrew word here is _dat_, which often means the legalistic aspects of religion. Here, however, it appears to mean “sect,” or in modern parlance, “movement.”
content.arabic: وينبغي أن نلفت النظر إلى ما قاله المقريزي «أن اليهود الربانين والقرائين تعارضوا بشأن ما كان بيد عنان «فالحقيقة أنه كان هناك بعض العلماء القدماء من القرائين قد عارضوا بعضاً من آراء عنان أعني أنهم لم يوافقوه في كل شيء ولكن معارضتهم كانت في المسائل الفرعية أما في المواضيع الأساسية فكانوا كلهم متفقين معه.

content.hebrew: פה להזכיר כי בימי רבנו ענן הנשיא הנגררים אחריו היו נקראים בתאר «ענניים», ורק אחרי עבור זמן מה אחריו, קבלו וקימו עליהם תאר «בני מקרא» או «הקראים» ומזה מובן כי התארים «ענניים» או «בני מקרא» או «קראים» אשר נפגוש בספרות, הם «שמות נרדפים».
content.english: It should also be noted here that in the days of R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi, his adherents were called “ʿAnanites”; it was only with the passage of time that they took for themselves the name “Scripturalists” or “Karaites.” And from this it is clear that the terms “ʿAnanites,” “Scripturalists,” and “Karaites,” which we find in the literature, are all synonyms.[95]
content.comments: [95] At some point, these terms might have been synonymous, but at least in the tenth century, the ʿAnanites and Karaites were two distinct groups. See Marina Rustow, _Heresy and the Politics of Community, The Jews of the Fatimid Caliphate_ (Ithaca and London: Cornell University Press, 2008), pp. 53ff. The epigraph page at the beginning of Rustow's book contains an English translation of a quote from Qirqisani's _Kitāb al-Anwār wa-al-Marāqib_, Book I, 10:1: “[Some of the disagreements between the Iraqi and Palestinian Rabbanites] make each group accuse the other of heresy. In fact, the religious divergence between the two groups is no smaller than that between both of them on the one hand and the Qaraites and the ʿAnanites on the other” (brackets in the original).
content.arabic: وفي أيام عنان كان أتباعه يعرفون باسم العنانيين ولكن بعد قليل من الزمن بعده أطلقوا على أنفسهم اسم «بني مقرا» أو «القرائين» ونفهم من ذلك أن العنانيين أو بني مقرا أو القرائين هي ألفاظ مترادفة.

content.hebrew:
בכל שבת ושבת בכל בתי כנסיות הקראים, אחר תפלת הבקר קוראים זכר מיוחד לרבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א, וזהו הנסח שלו:
{{quote:אלהינו ואלהי אבותינו ירחם את מתינו ואת מתיכם ואת מתי כלל כל עמו בית ישראל, בראש ובתחלה לרבנו ענן הנשיא איש האלהים ראש הגולה, אשר פתח את דרך התורה, והאיר עיני בני מקרא, ורבים השיב מעון ומעברה, והדריכנו בדרך ישרה, אלהי ישראל ילינהו במלון טוב ובמלון נחמד ובמלון נחשב, ועם הצדיקים הנוחלים בגן עדן. ויקים עליו מ״ש {{bible:וְהָיָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא שֹׁ֣רֶשׁ יִשַׁ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר עֹמֵד֙ לְנֵ֣ס עַמִּ֔ים אֵלָ֖יו גּוֹיִ֣ם יִדְרֹ֑שׁוּ וְהָיְתָ֥ה מְנֻחָת֖וֹ כָּבֽוֹד}} (ישעיה י״א 10) {{bible:א֭וֹיְבָיו אַלְבִּ֣ישׁ בֹּ֑שֶׁת וְ֝עָלָ֗יו יָצִ֥יץ נִזְרֽוֹ}} (תהלים קל״ב 18), ועוד יקים עליו מ״ש: {{bible:וְאַתָּ֖ה לֵ֣ךְ לַקֵּ֑ץ וְתָנ֛וּחַ וְתַעֲמֹ֥ד לְגֹרָלְךָ֖ לְקֵ֥ץ הַיָּמִֽין }}(דניאל י״ב 13).}}
content.english:
On every Sabbath, in every Karaite synagogue, a special commemorative prayer is recited for R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_ following the morning prayers.[98] This is its text:
{{quote:May our God and the God of our forefathers have mercy on our dead, on your dead, and on the dead of the entire nation of the House of Israel. First and foremost, in memory of R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi, man of God, the Exilarch, who opened the way of the Torah, and illuminated the eyes of the Karaites, and held back many from sin and iniquity,[96] and led us on a straight path.[97] May the God of Israel repose him in a good resting place, in a lovely resting place, in a dignified resting place, along with the righteous, who inherit Paradise. And may the verse that is written be fulfilled upon him: _And it shall come to pass in that day, that the root of Jesse, that standeth for an ensign of the peoples, unto him shall the nations seek; and his resting place shall be glorious_ (Isaiah 11:10). _His enemies will I clothe with shame; But upon himself shall his crown shine_ (Psalms 132:18). And may the verse that is written also be fulfilled upon him: _But go thou thy way till the end be; and thou shalt rest, and shalt stand up to thy lot, at the end of the days_ (Daniel 12:13).}}
content.comments: [98] This custom continues to this day in Karaite synagogues throughout Israel. | [96] Cf. Malachi 2:6. | [97] Cf. Psalms 107:7.
content.arabic:
وتخليداً لذكرى عنان اعتاد القراؤون في كل سبت في جميع كنائسهم عقب صلاة الصباح قراءة «زخير» خاص لعنان بهذا النص
{{quote:«إلهنا وإله آبائنا يرحم موتانا وموتاكم وموتى جميع شعبه بيت إسرائيل وفي مقدمتهم إمامنا الجليل عنان الناسي رجل الله ورأس الجالوت الذي فتح طريق الشريعة وأنار عيون القرائين وأرجع كثيراً من الناس عن طريق الخطايا وهدانا إلى السبيل القويم. إله إسرائيل بجعل مثواه مع الأبرار الذين سكنوا جنة عدن. ويثبت الله عليه آيته المقدسة {{quran:وَيَكُونُ فِي ذلِكَ الْيَوْمِ أَنَّ أَصْلَ يَسَّى الْقَائِمَ رَايَةً لِلشُّعُوبِ， إِيَّاهُ تَطْلُبُ الأُمَمُ， وَيَكُونُ مَحَلُّهُ مَجْدًا.}} (أشعيا ١١: ١٠). {{quran:أَعْدَاءَهُ أُلْبِسُ خِزْيًا， وَعَلَيْهِ يُزْهِرُ إِكْلِيلُهُ}} (مزامير ١٣٢: ١٨) كما يثبت عليه الآية المقدسة. {{quran:أَمَّا أَنْتَ فَاذْهَبْ إِلَى النِّهَايَةِ فتَسْتَرِيحَ， وتَقُومَ لِقُرعَتِكَ فِي نِهَايَةِ الأَيَّامِ}} (دانيال ١٢: ١٣).}}

content.hebrew:
ואחריו קוראים זכר לשלושה החכמים, והם מלמדי הקראים הראשונים, אשר עזרו אותו בשליחות הפצת דת הקראות בעולם, והם רבנו אפרים, ורבנו אלישע ורבנו חנכה, זכותם תגן עלינו, אמן.
החכם טוביה בן שמחה ז״ל לוי-בבוויץ׳
{{header:II מאמר על רבנו בנימן נהאונדי (המאה התשיעית למה״נ)}}
מאת החכם טוביה ן׳ שמחה ז״ל לוי-בבוויץ׳
בעיר אלקאהרה יע״א במצרים
בש׳ 1947 למה״נ
{{header:II ¶2.01רבנו בנימן נהאונדי בן משה מ״כ. (המאה התשיעית למה״נ)}}
content.english:
After this [prayer], they recite a memorial prayer for three [other] sages, who were teachers of the earlier Karaites and helped him (= ʿAnan) spread the Karaite faith around the world: R. Ephraim, R. Elisha, and R. Ḥanukka,[99] may their merits protect us, Amen.
_Ḥakham Ṭoviyya b. Simḥa (of blessed memory) Levi-Babovich_
{{header:II An Article on R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi (Ninth Century CE)}}
By: Ḥakham Ṭoviyya b. Simḥa Levi-Babovich
Cairo, Egypt
1947
content.comments: [99] The reader will recall that Ḥakham Ṭoviyya was specifically requested to expound upon these three obscure individuals. He gives us no information about them, and, indeed, not much is known. See also Abraham Baer Gottlober, _Biqqoret le-Toledot ha-Qaraʾim_ (Vilna, 1864), pp. 113, 124, 129, 139.
content.arabic:
وبعد قراءة هذا الدعاء يقرأ زخير على أرواح ثلاثة علماء من أنصار عنان المقربين إليه وهم أوائل معلمي القرائين الذين عاونوه في رسالته وهي نشر شريعة القرائين في العالم وهم سيدنا «أفرايم» وسيدنا «اليشاع» وسيدنا «حانوكا» ليكن ثوابهم شفيعاً لنا آمين.
**الحاخام طوبياه سمحاه ليفي بابوفتش**
{{header:مقالة عن أستاذنا **بنيامين النهاوندي** رحمه الله (القرن التاسع)}}
**بقلم الحاخام**
**طوبياه سمحاه ليفي بابوفيتش **
القاهرة سنة ١٩٤٧ إفرنجية
{{header:II ¶2.1**القسم الثاني** **أستاذنا بنيامين النهاوندي القاضي بن موسى رحمه الله** (من القرن التاسع)}}

content.english: {{header:II R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi b. Moses (Ninth Century CE)}}

content.hebrew: ויהי אחרי מות רבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א איש האלהים ראש הגולה, ירש כסאו בנו שאול הנשיא, ואחרי מות שאול הנשיא, לקח פקדתו בנו הבכור יאשיהו הנשיא. לשאול הנשיא היו שני בנים, הא׳ יאשיהו הנשיא אשר היו מפארים אותו בתארי הכבוד «נר הגולה וכליל התורה» (ראה ס׳ «אשכל הכפר», האלפא ביתא רנ״ח) והב׳ יחזקיהו הנשיא, אשר היו מתארים אותו בתאר הכבוד «מפתח הבינה» (ראה בס׳ «חלוק הקראים והרבנים» לרבנו אליהו בן אברהם המזרחי אשר חי במאה השתים עשרה למה״נ, אשר נדפס בס׳ «לקוטי קדמוניות» להחכם שמחה פינסקער, נספחים דף 106). והנה הם כלם היו חכמים, כאשר יעידו התארים אשר הכתירום בהם החכמים הבאים אחריהם, ובלי ספק כתבו חבורים שונים. אך לעגמת נפשנו חבוריהם לא הגיעו אלינו, יוכל היות מפני הסבה אשר זכרנו במאמרנו על רבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א, ר״ל מפני שמתנגדיהם הכחידו אותם מן הארץ.
content.english: Now, it came to pass after the death of R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi _yrʺe_,[100] the man of God and Exilarch, that his son Saul ha-Nasi inherited his seat, and after the passing of Saul ha-Nasi, he was succeeded by his firstborn son Josiah ha-Nasi. Saul ha-Nasi had two sons: the first, Josiah ha-Nasi, was adulated with many honorifics, including “Light of the Exile and Crown of the Torah” (see _Eshkol ha-Kofer_, Alphabet 258); and the second was Hezekiah ha-Nasi, who was described with the honorific “the Key to Understanding” (see_ Ḥilluq ha-Qaraʾim ve-ha-Rabbanim_ by R. Elijah b. Abraham ha-Mizraḥi, who lived in the twelfth century, which was published by the scholar Simḥa Pinsker in _Liqquṭé Qadmoniyyot_, appendices, p. 106). Now, they were all wise, as attested by the titles bestowed upon them by later sages, and they doubtlessly authored many works. However, to our great misfortune, none of their works have survived. Perhaps the reason for this is the same as the one that we have mentioned in our essay on R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi, namely, that their opponents wiped them off the face of the Earth.[101]
content.comments: [100] Cf. Joshua 1:1. | [101] See above, ¶1.25.
content.arabic: بعد وفاة إمامنا الجليل عنان الناسي رحمه الله ورث كرسيه ابنه شاؤول الناسي ثم بعد وفاة شاؤول خلفه ابنه البكر يوشياهو الناسي. وكان لشاؤول ولدان الأول يوشياهو وكانوا يصفونه احتراماً له بمصباح الجالوت وتاج التوراة انظر كتاب «أِشْكُول هَكُوفِر» أ.ب. ٢٥٨) والثاني حزقياهو الناسي وكانوا يصفونه احتراماً له بمفتاح الفهم (انظر كتاب افتراق القرائين والربانين لعالمنا الأستاذ إلياهو بن أبراهام همزراحي من القرن الثاني عشر وقد طبع هذا الكتاب ضمن كتاب «لقوطى قدمونيوت» لسِمْحَا بِنْسْكِر ملحق صفحة ١٠٦). وكانوا كلهم علماء كما تشهد بذلك الصفات التي كان ينعتهم بها العلماء الذين جاءوا بعدهم. ولا شك أنهم وضعوا مؤلفات مختلفة ولكنها مع الأسف لم تصل إلى أيدينا وقد يكون ذلك للسبب الذي ذكرناه في مقالنا عن عنان الناسي رحمه الله وهو أن خصومهم عملوا على محوها من الوجود.

content.hebrew: רבנו החכם סלמון בן ירוחים, אשר נכתוב על אודותיו גם כן מאמר מיוחד, בהקדמתו לפירושו על עשרת הדברים, שמר לנו דעת רבנו שאול הנשיא על הדבור הששי,{{bible: לֹ֖א תִּנְאָֽף}} (שמות כ׳ 14), אשר הוא היה מפרש אותו אזהרה כללית לכל מיני נאוף, בין באשת איש, בין בפנויה, נגד דעת קצת חכמים אחרים. (למשל רבנו מבורך בן נתן בן ניסן הלוי בחבורו «חטאנו» לליל יום הכפורים, המתחיל «מדוע נרים ראש לפני אל ולמה, לא נשכבה בבושה ונתכסה בכלמה» המפרש אותו אזהרה מגבלת, ר״ל רק ביחס לאשת איש.)
content.english: R. Salmon b. Yeruḥim (regarding whom we will write a separate essay), in the introduction to his commentary on the Decalogue, preserves Saul ha-Nasi's opinion on the Sixth Commandment,[102] _thou shalt not commit adultery_ (Exodus 20:14), which he explained, disagreeing with other sages, as a general prohibition regarding all types of adultery—whether with a married or unmarried woman. (For example, R. Mevorakh b. Nathan b. Nisan ha-Levi, in his _Ḥatanu_ poem[103] for the services of Yom Kippur night—which begins “How can we lift up our heads before God, and why are we not lying down in shame and covering ourselves in disgrace?”—explains it as being a limited injunction, applying only to a married woman.)
content.comments: [102] Ḥakham Ṭoviyya's listing of the prohibition on adultery as the Sixth Commandment might cause some confusion, because most Jews today deem the Sixth Commandment to be the prohibition against murder and the Seventh to be the prohibition against adultery. Ḥakham Ṭoviyya's enumeration is consistent with the Jewish tradition of Philo and Josephus (c. first century CE) and the Augustinian, Roman Catholic, and Lutheran traditions. In contrast, the Rabbinic, Greek Orthodox, and Protestant traditions count the prohibition against adultery as the Seventh Commandment. (See Moshe Weinfeld, _Deuteronomy 1–11: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary_ (The Anchor Bible) [New York: Doubleday, 1991], pp. 243f.) | [103] The term “_Ḥaṭanu_” refers to a genre of penitential poems. In the Karaite Yom Kippur service, the refrain of these poems is: “We have sinned (_ḥatanu_) with our forefathers; we have acted perversely and wickedly.” Amongst Rabbanites, the common refrain for this genre is: “We have sinned (_ḥatanu_), our Rock; forgive us, our Creator.” See Ezra Fleischer, _Hebrew Liturgical Poetry in the Middle Ages_ (Hebrew; Jerusalem: Keter Yerushalayim, 1975), pp. 203f.
content.arabic: إن أستاذنا سلمون بن يروحيم الذي سنفرد له مقالاً خاصاً وضع تفسيراً للعشر وصايا أورد لنا فيه رأي شاؤول الناسي في الوصية السادسة وهي {{quran:لاَ تَزْنِ}} (الخروج ٢٠: ١٤) ويقول إن شاؤول كان يفسرها بالنهي نهياً شاملاً عن كل أنواع الزنا سواء كان مع امرأة رجل أو امرأة خالية， وهذا مخالف لرأي بعض علمائنا الآخرين مثل أستاذنا مبوراح بن ناتان بن نيسان هليفي كما جاء في قصيدته التي تتلى في صلاة ليلة عيد الاستغفار التي مبدؤها «كيف نرفع رأسنا أمام الله وكيف لا نستر وجوهنا خجلاً» فقد فسر هذه الوصية بالنهي عن الزنا نهياً محدوداً فيما يتعلق بالمرأة المتزوجة.

content.hebrew: ומשֵם יאשיהו הנשיא הגיעו אלינו קטעי מאמרים, והם נזכרים בחבורי חז״ל הבאים אחריו. למשל בענין קנין האשה רבנו יאשיהו הנשיא אומר, שהאשה נקנית בששה דברים: במהר, בעדים, בכתב, בביאה, בקדושין, ובקנין (= שבועה), וגם רבנו יהודה הדסי בע״ס «אשכל הכפר» הביא ששה דברים והם: מהר, ארוש, כתב, עדים, ברית (= שבועה) וביאה. אבל רבנו זה בנימן נהאונדי הגבילם בחמשה דברים, והם: ארישה, לקיחה (= נשואין), מהר, ברית (= שבועה), עדים (ראה ס׳ גן עדן לרבנו אהרן ניקומידיאו, סדר נשים, פרק ששי).
content.english: As for Josiah ha-Nasi, only fragments of writings in his name have come down to us; they are mentioned in the works of our sages, of blessed memory,[104] who came after him. For instance, on the issue of acquiring a wife, R. Josiah ha-Nasi writes that a wife can be acquired in six ways: _mohar_,[105] witnesses, writing [a contract], consent,[106] betrothal, and acquisition (= oath).[107] Similarly, R. Judah Hadassi, author of _Eshkol ha-Kofer_, mentions six methods: _mohar_, betrothal, writing [a contract], witnesses, covenant (= oath), and intercourse.[108] However, R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi limits them to five, namely, betrothal, taking (= marriage), _mohar_, covenant (= oath), and witnesses. (See R. Aaron of Nicomedia, _Gan ʿEden_, Seder Nashim, Chapter 6.)
content.comments: [104] Ḥakham Ṭoviyya uses the acronym _Ḥazal_; see above in ¶1.15, footnote 6. Here, the reference is clearly to the Karaite sages. | [105] That is, a bridal payment for a virgin, often referred to as a “bride price.” On the connection between the biblical _mohar_ and the Rabbinic _ketuba_, see Deborah Greniman, “The Origins of the Ketubah: Deferred Payment or Cash up Front?” _Nashim_ 4 (2001): 84–118, and for the _mohar_ in the Middle Ages, see Mordechai Akiva Friedman, “The Minimum _Mohar_ Payment as Reflected in the Geniza Documents: Marriage Gift or Endowment Pledge?” _PAAJR_ 43 (1976): 15–47, and idem, _Jewish Polygyny in the Middle Ages_ (Mosad Bialik, 1986), passim. | [106] The Hebrew word that we have translated as “consent” is _biʾa_, from the root _b-w-ʾ_. Biblical Hebrew uses this to mean sexual intercourse, and Rabbanites followed suit. Karaites, however, use the word to refer to entering into a contract with consent. Cf. Aaron ben Elijah of Nicomedia, _Gan ʿEden_, Seder Nashim, ch. 6. The Arabic translation of _Rosh Pinna_ renders this as “acceptance” (_al-qabūl_). We note that the famed Karaite sage Judah Hadassi interpreted _biʾa_ to mean intercourse (see _Eshkol ha-Kofer,_ Alphabet 3, Letter _Ṭet_), and we have translated the following sentence accordingly. | [107] In this paragraph, the parenthetical remarks with an equal sign appear in the original Hebrew text by Ḥakham Ṭoviyya and are not editorial interventions. | [108] We have translated this according to Judah Hadassi's view that_ biʾa_ referred to intercourse, as described immediately above in footnote 104. We note, though, that the Arabic text here renders _biʾa_ as _al-qabūl_, suggesting that Ḥakham Ṭoviyya (or perhaps his Arabic translators) believed that it should be understood as “consent.”
content.arabic: أما عن يوشياهو الناسي فقد وصلت إلينا مقتطفات من أقواله ذكرت في مؤلفات علمائنا الذين جاءوا بعده منها مثلاً أن أركان الزواج ستة وهي المهر والشهود والكتاب والقبول والتقديس والقنيان (القسم) وأستاذنا يهودا هداسي (مؤلف كتاب أشكول هكوفر) اشترط أيضاً ستة شروط وهي المهر والخطبة والكتاب والشهود والعهد (القسم) والقبول. لكن أستاذنا بنيامين النهاوندي اقتصر على خمسة شروط وهي الخطبة والأخذ (التقديس) والمهر والعهد (القسم) والشهود (انظر كتاب جان عيدن لأستاذنا هارون نيكوميديو — باب النساء الفصل السادس).

content.hebrew: ומודעת לכל שהקראים כעת תחת ששה או חמשה התנאים האלה בשטר הקדושין כותבים בקצרה, רק שלושה תנאים, והם 1) מהר 2) כתב 3) וביאה.
content.english: It is widely known that Karaites today, instead of having these six or five conditions, write only three, in brief, in the marriage document: (1) _mohar_, (2) writing, and (3) consent.
content.arabic: ومما هو معروف أن القرائين في الوقت الحاضر يختصرون هذه الأركان إلى ثلاثة وهي المهر والكتاب والقبول.

content.hebrew: מהנאמר פה נראה, כי פעלת שאול הנשיא ובנו יאשיהו הנשיא לא כל כך היתה בולטת בתוך הגולה, אבל לעמת זאת, תלמיד ר׳ יאשיהו הנשיא והוא החכם בנימן נהאונדי, אשר אנחנו הולכים לספר עליו, הצטין מאד ביחס אל התפתחות דת הקראים.
content.english: From what has been said thus far, it is apparent that the activities of Saul ha-Nasi and his son Josiah ha-Nasi were not particularly prominent in the Exile.[109] On the other hand, Josiah's disciple, the sage Benjamin al-Nahawandi, whom we will discuss here, was widely acknowledged for his role in the development of the Karaite faith.
content.comments: [109] This is not to imply that the opinions of these sages were famous among the Jews of the Land of Israel but simply that most Jews of the time lived in the Diaspora, so if these sages' opinions were not famous among the Jews of the Diaspora, they were not famous among the Jews at all.
content.arabic: مما ذكرنا يتضح أن أثر شاؤول الناسي وابنه يوشياهو لم يكن بارزاً في الجالوت لكن بعكس ذلك فإن تلميذ يوشياهو الناسي وهو أستاذنا بنيامين النهاوندي كان ذا أثر عظيم في دعم وتقوية مذهب القرائين.

content.hebrew: החכם בנימן נהאונדי בן משה נ״ע, נולד בעיר נהאונדא, כאשר תעיד עליו התאר «נהאונדי», והיא אחת מערי מדי, אשר נגלו שמה עשרת השבטים אחר נפילת ממלכת ישראל. חי רבנו בנימן נהאונדי בעדות רבנו החכם יעקב קרקסאני בן יצחק (הנודע אצל החכמים בשם «אבו יוסוף יעקב») כשלשים או ארבעים שנה אחר רבנו ענן הנשיא בימי הכליף אל מעטאסים ביללאה (834-842 למה״נ), והיה תלמיד רבנו יאשיהו הנשיא, כאשר זכרנו למעלה, וגם עצמו העמיד תלמידים הרבה, וביניהם החכם הנודע דניאל אלקומיסי.
content.english: The sage Benjamin b. Moses al-Nahawandi (may his soul rest in Eden) was born in the city of Nahawand, as attested by the epithet “Nahawandi.” It is a city in Media, to which the Ten Tribes were exiled after the fall of the Kingdom of Israel. According to the testimony of the sage R. Jacob b. Isaac al-Qirqisani (who is known among scholars as “Abu Yusuf Yaʿqub”), he lived 30 or 40 years after R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi, in the days of Caliph al-Muʿṭasim Billah (r. 834–842); he was a disciple of Josiah ha-Nasi, as we have mentioned above; and he himself had many disciples, among them the famed sage Daniel al-Qumisi.
content.arabic: ولد أستاذنا بنيامين النهاوندي بن موسى في مدينة نهاونده كما يدل على ذلك وصفه بالنهاوندي وهي إحدى مدن ميديا وكان قد هاجر إليها عشرة أسباط بعد سقوط مملكة إسرائيل. وقد روى أستاذنا يعقوب القرقساني المعروف عند العلماء باسم أبي يوسف يعقوب أن أستاذنا بنيامين النهاوندي عاش ثلاثين أو أربعين عاماً بعد إمامنا الجليل عنان الناسي في عهد الخليفة المعتصم بالله ٨٣٤ — ٨٤٢ إفرنجية وكان تلميذاً ليوشياهو الناسي كما ذكرنا سالفاً. وقد تخرج على يدي النهاوندي كثير من التلاميذ منهم العالم المشهور دانييل القميصي.

content.hebrew: כנראה בנימן נהאונדי היה נושא מִשֹרת השופט או הדַיָּן בעירו נהאונדה, וחבר את ספרו «ס׳ הדינים», אשר נדבר עליו למטה, לצרכי היום, בשבתו על כסא המשפט. הוא היה כרוך מאד אחר רבנו ענן הנשיא יר״א, בפרשו את מצות תורתנו הק׳, וכאשר אומרים, «מפתו הוא היה אוכל, ומכוסו הוא היה שותה», ואם כי לא היה הולך אחריו שתום העין, ויעזר מאד לחזק את אָשְיות דת הקראים, עד כי חכמי הערב היו חושבים שהוא ג״כ ממיסדי דת הקראים, והיו קוראים את הקראים «אסחאב [צ״ל אצחאב] ענן ובנימן» (أصحاب عنان وبنيامين) ר״ל הנגררים אחרי ענן ובנימן, וקצת מחכמי אחינו הרבנים ג״כ חושבים את בנימן נהאונדי לאחד משלשה מיסדי דת הקראים, והם 1) רבנו ענן הנשיא 2) בנו שאול הנשיא 3) ובנימן נהאונדי.
content.english: It appears that Benjamin al-Nahawandi occupied the position of judge[110] in his hometown of Nahawand. While he occupied the bench of justice, he composed the _Book of Laws_, which we will discuss below, for day-to-day usage. He followed R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi very closely in his explication of the Torah's commandments; as the expression goes: “He ate of his bread and drank of his cup.”[111] However, he did not follow ʿAnan blindly. He was instrumental in establishing the foundations of the Karaite faith, to the extent that many Arab scholars considered him, too, to be one of the founders of Karaism; in fact, they referred to the group as _Aṣḥāb ʿAnān wa-Binyāmīn_, literally, “those who follow ʿAnan and Benjamin.” Some of our Rabbanite brethren likewise consider Benjamin al-Nahawandi to be one of the three founders of the Karaite faith: (1) ʿAnan ha-Nasi, (2) his son Saul ha-Nasi, and (3) Benjamin al-Nahawandi.
content.comments: [110] Ḥakham Ṭoviyya uses two Hebrew words for “judge” here, _shofeṭ_ and _dayyan_. If the two are not synonymous, the distinction is not obvious. | [111] Cf. II Samuel 12:3.
content.arabic: ويبدو أن بنيامين النهاوندي كان قاضياً أو حاكماً في بلده. وهناك ألف كتابه (القوانين) الذي سنتكلم عنه فيما بعد. وقد وضعه عندما كان قاضياً. وكان تابعاً أميناً لعنان الناسي في تفسيره لوصايا التوراة المقدسة فكان كما يقولون عنه يأكل من لقمته ويشرب من كأسه ولكنه مع ذلك لم يكن يتبعه اتباعاً أعمى. وقد ساهم كثيراً في تقوية أساس مذهب القرائين حتى أن علماء العرب كانوا يعدونه من مؤسسي مذهب القرائين وكانوا يسمون القرائين «بأصحاب عنان وبنيامين» أعني «اتباع عنان وبنيامين» كما أن بعضاً من علماء إخواننا الربانيين يعدون بنيامين أحد ثلاثة أسسوا مذهب القرائين وهم عنان الناسي وابنه شاؤول وبنيامين النهاوندي.

content.hebrew: רבנו בנימן נהאונדי בְּחֵרוּת הדעות היה הולך עד הקצה האחרון, והיה אומר, שבדבר הבנת מצות התורה יש זכות להַתַּלמיד להתנגד לדעת מלמדו, הבן יתנגד לאביו, ולא יאמר האב, למה החלפת דברי, וכן האח הצעיר יתנגד לאחיו הגדול, אם רק יוכל לחזק את דעתו בדברי התנ״ך. ובזה הוא הלך אחרי חכמינו הקדמונים ז״ל, אשר היה מאמר שגור בפיהם «במקום שיש חלול השם אין חולקין כבוד אפילו לרב».
content.english: R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi took freedom of opinion to the extreme. He would say that [when one endeavors] to understand the Torah's commandments, a disciple has the right to oppose the opinion of his teacher, and a son can contradict his father, and the father may not say: “Why are you contesting my word?” Also, a younger brother may oppose the older, as long as he can buttress his position from the words of Scripture. And in this, he followed the axiom established by our early sages, of blessed memory, who were wont to say: “Whenever there is a desecration of the name of God, one does not accord honor even to a master.”[112]
content.comments: [112] In fact, this quote is not from early Karaite sages but from the Babylonian Talmud,_ Berakhot_ 19b.
content.arabic: كان أستاذنا بنيامين يذهب في حرية الرأي إلى أبعد حد وكان يقول فيما يختص بتفسير التوراة أنه يجوز للتلميذ أن يعارض أستاذه， وللابن أن يعارض أباه وليس للأب أن يسأل ابنه لماذا خالفت رأيي وكذلك يحق للأخ الصغير أن يناقش أخاه الأكبر， كل هذا بشرط أن يؤيد كل واحد رأيه بآيات من الكتاب المقدس. وفي هذا الصدد اتبع النهاوندي رأي علمائنا الأقدمين الذين كانوا يتمثلون بالمثل العبري القديم الذي معناه إذا استهين بالله فلا محل حتى لاحترام الأستاذ.

content.hebrew: בזמן רבנו בנימן נהאונדי, התחילו הנגררים אחרי ענן הנשיא לקרוא את עצמם «בני מקרא» או «קראים» ולא «ענניים», כאשר היה לפנים.
content.english: It was during the lifetime of R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi that the followers of ʿAnan ha-Nasi began to call themselves “Scripturalists” or “Karaites” and no longer “ʿAnanites.”
content.arabic: وفي أيام بنيامين بدأ اتباع عنان يسمون أنفسهم بني مقرا أو قرائين， لا عنانيين كما كان يطلق عليهم قبل.

content.hebrew: רבנו בנימן נהאונדי כתב את רב חבוריו בל׳ הקדש, להפך מן רבנו ענן הנשיא אשר היה כותב את כל חבוריו בל׳ ארמית, כאשר זכרנו במאמרנו אשר כתבנו על אודותיו, ולהפך גם מן הבאים אחריו, אשר היו כותבים רב חבוריהם בל׳ ערבית ולא בל׳ הקדש, וכונתי פה על חכמי הקראים הדרים במצרים, בארץ ישראל, בארם (סורייא) ובבבל, ובכלל בארצות המזרח, אשר בהן הלשון הערבית היא המתהלכת בתוך העם, וזה עד סוף המאה החמש עשרה, ואחרי כן כמעט כל חכמי הקראים בכל הארצות כתבו חבוריהם בל׳ הקדש.
content.english: R. Benjamin al-Nahawandi wrote most of his works in Hebrew, unlike R. ʿAnan ha-Nasi, who wrote all of his works in Aramaic, as we mentioned in the essay devoted to him,[113] and also unlike most subsequent sages, who wrote most of their works in Arabic and not Hebrew. I am referring specifically to the Karaite sages who lived in Egypt, the Land of Israel, Aram (Syria),[114] Babylonia, and the East in general, where the Arabic language was widely spoken by the people. This [state of affairs] lasted until the end of the fifteenth century, after which almost all Karaite sages, in all lands, wrote their works exclusively in Hebrew.[115]
content.comments: [113] See above, ¶1.24. | [114] Parentheses in the original text. | [115] According to Marina Rustow, after ʿAnan, the Karaites generally abandoned Aramaic, “which was too burdened with the Talmudic past and now became the sole province of the Rabbanite camp. Instead, they turned their attention to Hebrew, the language of the Bible, and to Arabic, the new lingua franca of scholarly endeavor. The result of this shift was an outpouring of grammatical and exegetical work occasioned by the renaissance of Hebrew study and a stream of Arabic Bible translations and commentaries that would profoundly affect the history of Medieval Jewish Biblical exegesis” (_Scripture and Schism_, p. 63).
content.arabic: وقد ألف أستاذنا النهاوندي معظم كتبه باللغة العبرية بخلاف إمامنا الجليل عنان فقد وضع كتبه باللغة الآرامية «الكلدانية» وبعكس من جاء بعده من علماء القرائين فقد وضعوا أكثر كتبهم باللغة العربية لا باللغة العبرية وأقصد هنا علماء القرائين الذين أقاموا في مصر وأرض إسرائيل وسوريا والعراق والشرق عموماً حيث كانت اللغة العربية هي اللغة المستعملة لغاية آخر القرن الخامس عشر. أما بعد ذلك فإن معظم العلماء القرائين كانوا يضعون كتبهم باللغة العبرية.

content.hebrew: מכל חבורי בנימן נהאונדי מעטים הגיעו אלינו בשלמות, ומביניהם ס׳ הדינים שלו, והוציאה אותו לאור חברת הקראים מעמידי הדפוס בש׳ תקצ״ד לפ״ק (1834 למה״נ) בעיר גוזלווא יע״א ברוסייא, ביחד עם ס׳ «מבחר ישרים» לרבנו אהרן הראשון, וס׳ «העֹשר» לרבנו יעקב בן ראובן נ״ע — והם פירושים על ספרי נביאים וכתובים. וההוצאה הזאת נמצאת אצלנו פה באוצר ספרי בית הדין.
content.english: Of all the literary output of Benjamin al-Nahawandi, very little has come down to us in full. Among [this] is his _Book of Laws_, which was published by the Karaite Society of Supporters of the Press in the year 5594 (1834 CE) in the city of Gozlova,[116] Russia, together with _Mivḥar Yesharim_ by R. Aaron I and _Sefer ha-ʿOsher_ by R. Jacob b. Reuben (may their souls rest in Eden), both commentaries on the Prophets and Writings. This publication can be found here in the library of our Religious Court.
content.comments: [116] Today known as “Eupatoria” or “Yevpatoria.”
content.arabic: ومما يؤسف له أن مؤلفات النهاوندي لم يصل إلى أيدينا إلا القليل منها كاملاً ومن بينها أيضاً كتاب «القوانين» وقد طبعته جمعية نشر مخطوطات القرائين بمدينة جزلوفا بروسيا سنة ٥٥٩٤ للخليقة — ١٨٣٤ إفرنجية مع كتاب مبحار يشاريم لأستاذنا هارون الأول وكتاب «سيفر هعوشر» لأستاذنا يعقوب بن روبين وهما كتابان في تفسير كتب الأنبياء وباقي الكتاب المقدس عندنا وهذه الطبعة موجودة لدينا بمكتبة دار الشرع عند العلماء المتأخرين.

content.hebrew: ס׳ הדינים הזה נודע אצל החכמים האחרונים בשם «מַשְׂאַת בנימן». וכולל בתוכו דיני ממונות ודיני נפשות ואחרים, אשר הם באו בו בלי סדר מעוין, מעורבים אלה באלה, כאשר הוא אצל רב החכמים הקדמונים. בראש ס׳ הדינים הוא כותב הרבה על חובות השופטים והעדים, ועל כל דין ודין הוא מביא סיוע מן הכתוב, מן התנ״ך. ומצוין בס׳ הדינים הזה, כי הוא חותם אותו באמרו, כי אין חשש אם ישתמשו בני מקרא בדינים אשר לא זכר אותם בספרו ואשר הם נהוגים אצל הרבנים, אם בדינים האלה אין מחלקת בינינו ובינם.
content.english: The _Book of Laws_ is known among the more recent sages under the name _Masʾat Binyamin_. It includes laws about monetary matters, laws about capital crimes, and more. They are all recorded there in no specific order, with the various topics interspersed, as is the case with [the writings of] most early sages. At the beginning of his _Book of Laws_, he writes at length about the obligations of judges and witnesses, and for every rule, he brings a verse from Scripture for support. It is worth noting that he concludes the book by saying that there is no problem if Karaites use rulings that are not mentioned in the book but rather are practiced by Rabbanites, as long as there is no disagreement between them and us [about the given issue].
content.arabic: أما كتاب القوانين فمعروف باسم «مسآت بنيامين» ومعناه هدية بنيامين ويحتوى على أحكام الجنح والجنايات وقد وردت في الكتاب غير مرتبة كما جرى عليه أكثرية العلماء الأقدمين. وفي صدر كتاب القوانين شرح بنيامين تفصيلياً واجبات القضاة والشهود. أما بنود الأحكام فكان يؤيد كلا منها بآية من الكتاب المقدس. ومما يلفت النظر في كتاب القوانين هذا أن بنيامين ختمه بقوله إنه لا بأس من أن يجري القراؤون على أحكام لم يذكرها في كتابه ويجري عليها الربانون بشرط ألا يكون هناك خلاف بيننا وبينهم فيها.

content.hebrew:
נעיר פה על קצת דינים מהספר הזה, אשר בקצתם דעת רבנו ענן הנשיא ודעת החכמים האחרונים משֻנה מן דעתו.
